summary: Odyssey is a browser game that teaches spacecraft engineering through Moon, Mars, and Europa missions. Players assemble a spacecraft, inspect live trade-offs, respond to a mission event, and review which engineering decisions helped their observations reach Earth.
details:
Space missions are familiar as stories of exploration. The constraints behind them are harder to see. Odyssey makes those decisions tangible for students, educators, and curious players. Each mission starts with a scientific objective and explicit engineering limits. In the hangar, changing an engine, instrument, tank, power source, or radio updates mass, ideal velocity change, thrust-to-weight, power margin, and mission readiness.

After launch, an interactive trajectory shows the next checkpoint. Each reachable destination presents a decision that changes power demand, available solar power, or the amount of data returned. The debrief shows which requirements passed and where the mission fell short. Players can save two designs, compare trade-offs, explore hypothetical changes without modifying their draft, and ask a rule-based Copilot to explain a specific result. The guided lunar mission provides a reproducible walkthrough without an account.

The model uses illustrative hardware and a single-stage vertical ascent sample. It treats transfer and science operations as educational scenarios. Future work could add staging, trajectory windows, and explicit radio link budgets. The Delta-V Odyssey project contributors are Mark Mohsen, Bola Gehad, David Farid, Doaa Adel, and Ruqia Farid.

NASA Data

The app uses NASA Glenn educational references for the ideal rocket equation, thrust-to-weight ratio, specific impulse, and mass ratios. The NASA mission comparison uses public Apollo 11, Mars Pathfinder/Sojourner, and Europa Clipper materials for historical context, instruments, propulsion roles, power and communications. The app does not ingest live NASA telemetry. The game catalog, credit values, solar multipliers, radio classes, and mission thresholds are illustrative. NASA Glenn: https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/beginners-guide-to-aeronautics/ideal-rocket-equation/ and https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/beginners-guide-to-aeronautics/thrust-to-weight-ratio/. Mission references: https://www.nasa.gov/mission/apollo-11/, https://science.nasa.gov/mission/mars-pathfinder/, and https://science.nasa.gov/mission/europa-clipper/.

Space Agency Partner & Other Data

The game uses original illustrative hardware, event assumptions, and artwork. It was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber and Motion. The interface uses Lucide icons and the Inter, Space Grotesk and JetBrains Mono fonts. Game sound effects use the Web Audio API. No external mission dataset from a space-agency partner was integrated.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

OpenAI Codex assisted with writing, reviewing, and testing application code, drafting documentation and producing the programmatically drawn SVG and CSS illustrations used in the app and web slides. ImageGen produced original astronaut and destination concept art, marked in the interface, and the labeled Delta-V team illustration featuring the Egyptian flag. The local pitch uses actual gameplay recordings, synthesized English narration and Arabic subtitles. The in-game Odyssey AI Copilot uses deterministic rules and the current spacecraft evaluation. The release contains no live LLM, external inference service, or API key.
